claims.claim: The Understanding by Design framework plans backward through three stages - Stage 1 identify desired results, Stage 2 determine acceptable assessment evidence, Stage 3 plan learning experiences and instruction - and treats alignment as a key concept: the Stage 1 content and understanding must be what is assessed in Stage 2 and taught in Stage 3.

Wiggins and McTighe present backward design as a way to avoid what they call the twin sins of activity-oriented and coverage-oriented curriculum planning, and report having observed that curriculum planning often translates into listing activities (Stage 3) with only a general sense of intended results and little attention to assessment evidence (Stage 2).

The authors of Understanding by Design chose the unit rather than the single lesson as the focus of design and state that they do not recommend isolated lesson planning separate from unit planning, because understandings, essential questions and transfer performance tasks are too complex to be addressed within a single lesson; they add that teachers often report that attention to Stages 1 and 2 sharpens their lesson planning.

Madeline Hunter wrote in 1985 that her elements - which she called a 'white sauce recipe' when misapplied - were designed to help teachers plan, that in no way can a teacher be judged by the inclusion of all those elements, that many lessons will incorporate only a few, and that any observer who uses a checklist to make sure a teacher is using all seven elements does not understand the model.

Hunter described her work as a clinical theory of instruction premised on the teacher as decision maker, whose purpose was to tell teachers what to consider before deciding what to do, and said models should be judged on their ability to guide behavior, predict outcomes and stimulate research rather than on being the final answer.

Published enumerations of Hunter's lesson-design elements do not agree: Hunter's own 1985 article refers to 'all seven elements', while a university reference page lists eight - anticipatory set, purpose, input, modeling, guided practice, checking for understanding, independent practice and closure.

Gagne's nine events of instruction are: gain attention of the students, inform students of the objectives, stimulate recall of prior learning, present the content, provide learning guidance, elicit performance (practice), provide feedback, assess performance, and enhance retention and transfer.

Rosenshine states that his principles of instruction come from three sources - research in cognitive science, research on the classroom practices of master teachers whose classrooms made the highest achievement gains, and research on cognitive supports such as thinking aloud, scaffolds and models - and that the agreement among these three different bodies of research is what gives him confidence in the findings. The article presents ten principles.

Rosenshine reports that the optimal success rate for fostering student achievement appears to be about 80 percent, and cites a study of fourth-grade mathematics in which 82 percent of students' answers were correct in the classrooms of the most successful teachers while the least successful teachers had a success rate of only 73 percent.

In the classroom studies Rosenshine summarizes, less successful teachers gave much shorter presentations and explanations and then passed out worksheets, while the most successful teachers spent more time in guided practice, asking questions, checking for understanding and correcting errors; where guided practice was too short, students were not prepared for seatwork and made more errors during independent practice.

Rosenshine reports that effective teachers checked for understanding by asking students to summarize the presentation so far, repeat directions or procedures, or say whether they agreed or disagreed with another student's answer, whereas less effective teachers simply asked 'Are there any questions?' and, hearing none, assumed students had learned the material and passed out worksheets.

The IES What Works Clearinghouse and its expert panel assigned a strong level of evidence, based on 43 studies, to providing systematic instruction during elementary mathematics intervention; the recommendation's steps are to review and integrate previously learned content, use accessible numbers when introducing new concepts and procedures, sequence instruction so the mathematics builds incrementally, provide visual and verbal supports, and provide immediate supportive feedback that addresses misunderstandings.

The IES What Works Clearinghouse assigned a strong level of evidence, based on eleven studies of students in grades 6-12, to explicitly teaching writing strategies using a Model-Practice-Reflect instructional cycle in which the teacher models a strategy, students practice it, and students then evaluate their own writing and strategy use.

In the same secondary writing practice guide, the recommendation to use assessments of student writing to inform instruction and feedback received only a minimal level of evidence: four studies contributed, all found positive effects on at least one writing outcome, but none provided a direct test of the recommendation because the interventions also included components outside it.

The IES practice guide Organizing Instruction and Study to Improve Student Learning assigned a strong level of evidence to using quizzes to re-expose students to key content, based on nine experimental studies with K-12 students, more than 30 experimental studies with college students, and a large body of controlled laboratory experiments on the testing effect.

The How People Learn consensus report's first key finding is that students come to the classroom with preconceptions about how the world works, and that if their initial understanding is not engaged they may fail to grasp the new concepts and information taught, or may learn them for purposes of a test but revert to their preconceptions outside the classroom.

The widely repeated pacing claim that student attention declines about 10 to 15 minutes into a lecture is not well supported: Wilson and Korn reviewed the underlying research and reported that it provides little support for the belief, and that the studies failed to account for individual differences in attention.

A common practical lesson template divides a class period into an introduction that activates prior knowledge, learning activities, and a closure that summarizes or gathers formative feedback, treats the lesson as one component of a larger unit, and advises planning at least one point per lesson at which the instructor receives feedback on student learning.

Checks for understanding serve two planning purposes at once: the retrieval they require is itself instructionally valuable, and they tell the teacher whether misunderstandings are forming while there is still time in the period to address them.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How long one segment of a lesson should run before the teacher changes mode.
positions: Practical teaching-center guidance commonly recommends organizing a period into roughly 20-minute learning episodes to sustain engagement.
Wilson and Korn's review found that the research behind the standard 10-to-15-minute attention-decline claim provides little support for it and generally ignored individual differences.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents segmenting as a planning heuristic that stops any single mode from over-running, and states explicitly that the attention-span number underneath it is not well evidenced. No fixed attention span is asserted.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The evidential status of named lesson-planning frames (Hunter's elements, Gagne's nine events).
positions: Both frames are widely taught in teacher preparation and were widely mandated in supervision and evaluation systems.

Hunter herself objected that judging a teacher by the presence of all seven elements misreads the model, published enumerations of her elements disagree, and neither frame carries a WWC-style effectiveness rating as a package.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson labels both as historical planning frames - checklists of things a plan might address - and anchors every effectiveness claim about instructional sequence to the IES/WWC practice guides and to Rosenshine's synthesis instead.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether backward design belongs at the level of the single lesson.
positions: Backward design is routinely taught and used as a lesson-planning method.
Wiggins and McTighe chose the unit as the design focus and say they do not recommend isolated lesson planning separate from unit planning.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson applies the backward-design logic at lesson level - result, then evidence, then activity - while stating plainly that the framework's own authors locate the design work at the unit and see the lesson as nested inside it.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strongly evidence-based practice guides support the classroom sequence described here.
positions: Systematic instruction and the Model-Practice-Reflect cycle each carry a strong evidence rating.

Those ratings are for specified practices with specified populations - elementary mathematics intervention, grades 6-12 writing - not for a general lesson template, and within the same writing guide a neighbouring recommendation earned only minimal evidence.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states each rating together with its population and study count, and does not claim that a generic lesson-anatomy template inherits those ratings.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted nothing substantive about lesson planning; its body text was template boilerplate ('Lesson Planning is a foundational concept in Education', 'a label on a toolbox drawer') with no sources, no worked example and no named framework, and was discarded in full.
The draft's three quick-check questions tested generic study-skills advice rather than lesson planning and were discarded.
The draft carried an empty sources array while being presented as a lesson; nothing in it was verifiable.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with researched content built on backward design, historical planning frames, lesson anatomy, pacing, planned checks, misconception anticipation and contingency.
Stated Rosenshine's principles as a synthesis of three research literatures rather than as experimental findings, per the article's own framing.
Attached population and study counts to every WWC evidence rating cited, so no rating is read as a general endorsement of a lesson template.
Recorded that Hunter's own 1985 article rejects checklist use of her elements, and that published enumerations of those elements disagree (seven in her own wording, eight on the CSUN reference page).
Refused to assert the common '10 to 15 minute attention span' pacing rule; presented segmenting as a heuristic and cited Wilson and Korn on the weakness of the underlying research.

Corrected the success-rate figures carried in the quarantined draft: Rosenshine's fourth-grade mathematics contrast is 82 percent for the most successful teachers versus 73 percent for the least successful, with about 80 percent given as the optimal rate.

Reused the existing source-registry identifiers wwc-assisting-students-struggling-mathematics-2021, ies-wwc-secondary-writing-2016, wwc-organizing-instruction-2007 and nrc-how-people-learn-2000 with their registered URLs, in place of the new duplicate ids the quarantined packet had invented.
Kept formative assessment strictly at the level of planning in-period checks, and kept objective-writing mechanics and Bloom's taxonomy out, to respect topic ownership.
